Here is what the picture shows. It is a vertical bar graph. On the bottom axis you can see the five types of school supplies: pencils, scales, pens, sharpeners, and erasers. Above that, the left‑hand side shows a vertical scale that counts how many of each item there are. Each category has its own bar that rises from the baseline. The height of the bar matches the number written next to it with a red dashed line and an arrow pointing to that number on the scale. 

The amounts shown are: eight pencils, three scales, two pens, five sharpeners, and four erasers. The bars are evenly spaced along the horizontal axis. The axis labels and numbers are clear, though the exact scale markings are not fully readable because of the image’s resolution. The title of the chart is “Untitled.”

The diagram shows a simple light‑sensing circuit. It uses a 9‑volt battery as the power source. The light‑dependent resistor, or LDR, is connected in series with a 100‑kilo‑ohm variable resistor, called R2. These two components form a voltage divider that changes the voltage sent to the base of a BC547 NPN transistor. The transistor acts like a switch; when enough base voltage is present it turns on and allows current to flow from its collector to its emitter. That current passes through a fixed 390‑ohm resistor, R1, and then through an LED. So when the LDR senses light, its resistance drops, the base voltage rises, the transistor turns on, and the LED lights up. When it is dark the LDR’s resistance is high, the base voltage drops, the transistor turns off, and the LED turns off. This is a basic example of a light‑activated switch circuit.
How many resistors are there in the circuit?
There are three resistors in the circuit. That includes the light‑dependent resistor, the 390‑ohm fixed resistor, and the 100‑kilo‑ohm variable resistor.
Happened if I replaced the battery with 16 volt source.

If you swap the 9‑volt battery for a 16‑volt supply, a few things in that simple light‑activated circuit will change.

First, the voltage across the LED and its series resistor, R1, will increase. The transistor will still turn on when the LDR lets enough base voltage through, so the LED will still light. But now the collector‑to‑emitter voltage when the transistor is on will be almost the full 16 V minus the small drop across the transistor (about 0.2 V). That leaves roughly 15.8 V to be shared by the LED and the 390‑ohm resistor.

If the LED’s forward voltage is about 2 V, the 390‑ohm resistor will drop the rest. 13.8 V across 390 ohms gives a current of about 35 mA. Most small LEDs are rated for 20 mA maximum, so the LED could overheat or even burn out. The transistor (BC547) can handle up to about 100 mA, so it might survive the extra current, but it will be closer to its limit and could overheat too.

Second, the base current will also increase because the base‑to‑emitter junction sees a higher voltage difference. That might push the transistor into a higher saturation level, but it could also stress the base‑emitter junction if the base resistor or R2 value isn’t adjusted.

So the main practical outcome is that the LED and possibly the transistor could get overloaded. To keep the circuit safe, you’d either need to use a higher‑value resistor in series with the LED, add a base resistor, or keep the supply at 9 V.
